findings.title: Dunder/eval bans bypassed via `__builtins__` Name or string-based attribute access
findings.desc: The dunder check only inspects `ast.Attribute` nodes and BAD_NAMES omits `__builtins__`, so `__builtins__.exec("...")` passes the gate outright; approved `operator.attrgetter("__class__")` similarly evades via uninspected string arguments. This defeats the specifically-claimed "names eval/exec/…" and "dunder attribute access" enforcements, though the doc's "not a sandbox" caveat partially mitigates.

findings.title: open() write-mode check silently passes non-literal modes
findings.desc: The mode check only examines `ast.Constant` arguments; `open(path, mode_var)` or any computed mode (e.g. `"w" if c else "r"`) leaves `mode=None` and is allowed, bypassing the claimed "enforced, not eyeballed" block of non-read-mode opens.

findings.title: Over-broad BAD_ATTRS rejects legitimate approved-module usage
findings.desc: Blocking bare attribute names `load`/`loads`/`replace`/`rename` rejects `json.load(s)`, `str.replace`, `datetime.replace`, and `DataFrame.rename` — all common, safe operations in approved modules. It also contradicts the doc's claim that only `np.load(..., allow_pickle=True)` is blocked, since every `.load` attribute is rejected.

findings.title: Large-int results crash the evaluator's print on Python ≥3.11
findings.desc: Results exceeding the 4300-digit int→str cap (reachable under MAX_EXP=1000, e.g. `99999**1000`) raise ValueError at print time, producing a false "rejection" for a valid expression.

findings.title: Security model overstates Mode 1 resource limits
findings.desc: "Both run under `timeout` + `ulimit`" is inaccurate: the Mode 1 invocation (line 72) uses `timeout 5` only, with no `ulimit`.

findings.title: File-write enforcement claim is misleading; residual-risk note omits write primitive
findings.desc: Arbitrary file writes remain trivially available via approved APIs (`DataFrame.to_csv`, `np.savetxt`, `plt.savefig`, `Workbook.save`), so "filesystem-write methods … enforced by check.py" overstates coverage, and the residual-risk paragraph (line 32) discloses file-read/exec risks but not file-overwrite risk.

findings.title: eval/exec banned only as bare names — trivial checker bypass
findings.desc: The gate rejects `eval`/`exec`/`getattr` only as `ast.Name`, so `__builtins__.eval("__import__('os').system('id')")` passes (the name `__builtins__` isn't banned, attribute `.eval` isn't in BAD_ATTRS, and string payloads are never inspected). Same class: `pandas.eval(...)` / `df.query(...)`. This is a one-liner RCE/exfil, not the "edge-case" the residual-risk note implies.

findings.title: Exponent cap doesn't prevent memory DoS; Mode 1 lacks the ulimit the docs claim
findings.desc: MAX_EXP only bounds each single exponent, so parenthesized nesting like `((9**1000)**999)**999` (each exponent ≤ 1000) still produces exponentially sized integers, contradicting the "can't exhaust CPU/memory" comment. Compounding it, the Security model says "Both run under `timeout` + `ulimit`" but Mode 1 (line 72) runs with `timeout` only — no `-v` address-space cap.

findings.title: Predictable heredoc delimiter allows breakout
findings.desc: The anti-injection guarantee assumes the untrusted body never contains a line equal to the delimiter (`EXPREOF`/`PYEOF`); attacker-influenced multi-line input containing such a line terminates the heredoc early and the remaining lines execute as shell commands. A random per-invocation delimiter (or delimiter-collision check) is needed for the "inert body" claim to hold.

findings.title: `load`/`loads` attribute ban kills approved modules' primary APIs
findings.desc: Banning attributes `load`/`loads` rejects `json.load`/`json.loads` — the main API of the explicitly approved `json` module — and safe `np.load(..., allow_pickle=False)`; it also makes the `allow_pickle` keyword check (lines 145-147) dead code. The "Blocked patterns" doc section doesn't disclose this, so sanctioned scripts will be rejected.

findings.title: open() write-mode check only resolves literal constants
findings.desc: `mode` is only read from `ast.Constant`, so `m = "w"; open(path, m)` (or any computed mode) bypasses the write-mode ban and permits arbitrary file writes within the rlimits. Low given the stated defense-in-depth framing, but it undercuts the "machine-enforced" claim for this control.

findings.title: `ulimit -v 2000000` can spuriously kill legitimate approved imports
findings.desc: A ~2GB virtual-memory cap is tight for the sanctioned scientific stack — numpy/pandas/matplotlib with OpenBLAS thread stacks routinely inflate vsize — so valid scripts may die with MemoryError at import and look like rejections. Consider a higher cap or `-m`/`-s`-style limits instead.

findings.title: `operator.attrgetter`/`methodcaller` fully bypass the attribute checks
findings.desc: The checker only inspects `ast.Attribute` nodes for dunder/dangerous attrs and `ast.Name` for banned builtins, but `operator` is allowlisted — `attrgetter("__init__.__globals__")` (or `from operator import attrgetter`) performs arbitrary attribute traversal via plain calls with string arguments, enabling the classic `__subclasses__`/`__globals__` walk to code execution. This defeats the "machine-enforced gate" claim even before the residual-risk disclaimer; at minimum block `operator.attrgetter`/`methodcaller` or scan string constants for dunder paths.

findings.title: open()-mode and allow_pickle checks are literal-only
findings.desc: `open(path, mode_var)` with a non-constant mode, and `allow_pickle=1` (or any non-literal truthy) bypass the gate, since only `ast.Constant` arguments and `value is True` are examined — contradicting the documented claim that non-read `open()` and pickle deserialization are machine-blocked.

findings.title: BAD_ATTRS over-blocks common safe methods of allowlisted modules
findings.desc: Blanket attribute bans on `load`/`loads` (json.load/loads — json is allowlisted and read-safe), `replace` (str.replace, DataFrame.replace), `rename` (DataFrame.rename), `run`, `call`, and `touch` will reject large classes of legitimate Mode-2 scripts; the docs also claim only `np.load(..., allow_pickle=True)` is a deserialization sink, which no longer matches the implemented behavior.

findings.title: Mode 1 runs without ulimit and MAX_EXP doesn't bound result size
findings.desc: The security model states "Both run under `timeout` + `ulimit`," but Mode 1's invocation has no ulimit; and the exponent cap only checks each Pow node's right operand, so left-nested powers like `((9**1000)**1000)**1000` (~10^9-digit ints, hundreds of MB) are permitted with only a 5s wall-clock limit against memory exhaustion.

findings.title: pandas `.eval`/`.query` reachable despite `eval` ban
findings.desc: `eval` is banned only as a bare name and `.eval` is not in BAD_ATTRS, so `pd.eval(...)`/`df.eval(...)` on attacker-influenced strings passes the gate — pandas itself warns eval is unsafe on untrusted input, and this is inconsistent with blocking `sympify`/`parse_expr` for the same reason.

findings.title: Fixed heredoc delimiters allow shell injection
findings.desc: Quoting a heredoc disables expansion but does not prevent attacker-controlled input from containing `EXPREOF` or `PYEOF` on its own line, terminating the heredoc and executing subsequent text as shell commands. findings.title: Static gate is trivially bypassable
findings.desc: Attribute bans can be bypassed with allowed imports such as `from pandas import read_pickle`, and `allow_pickle` validation accepts truthy non-`True` values such as `1` or computed expressions; dynamic or computed `open()` modes similarly bypass write checks. These permit the deserialization RCE and filesystem writes the checker claims to block.

findings.title: Receiver-blind attribute bans reject benign supported code
findings.desc: Every attribute named `load`, `loads`, `replace`, or `run` is rejected regardless of its receiver, so ordinary approved operations such as `json.loads(...)` and string `.replace(...)` fail. This conflicts with the approved-module documentation and makes the scientific mode unnecessarily unusable.

findings.title: Bare arithmetic lacks the promised memory limit
findings.desc: Mode 1 uses only `timeout`, despite the security model stating both modes run under `timeout` and `ulimit`; nested powers with individually permitted exponents can allocate enormous integers before the wall-clock timeout terminates the process. This exposes the host to memory exhaustion.

findings.title: RCE bypass via attribute access of restricted names
findings.desc: The static checker correctly blocks restricted functions (e.g., `eval`, `exec`) when invoked as direct variables (`ast.Name`), but fails to inspect them when accessed as attributes on objects (e.g., `__builtins__.eval()`, `pd.eval()`). This allows immediate sandbox escape and arbitrary code execution by leveraging allowed namespaces.

findings.title: Arbitrary file write via dynamic `open()` mode bypass
findings.desc: The `open()` validation assumes the file mode is explicitly provided as a literal `ast.Constant` string. An attacker can assign the write mode to a variable prior to the function call (e.g., `m='w'; open('f', m)`) to bypass the filter entirely and overwrite locally accessible files.

findings.title: Deserialization RCE bypass for `allow_pickle`
findings.desc: The `allow_pickle` safety check strictly ensures the argument is explicitly the boolean literal `True` by using `is True`. Supplying the equivalent truthy arguments like integers (`allow_pickle=1`) or storing it in variables (`p=True; np.load(..., allow_pickle=p)`) silently evades the check, enabling RCE.

findings.title: Incomplete blocklist allows local file writes via allowed libraries
findings.desc: Although generic filesystem methods (e.g., `write_text`, `unlink`) are explicitly blocked, native file-writing methods belonging to the explicitly allowed modules (`to_csv`, `to_excel`, `to_json`, `numpy.save`) are completely excluded from `BAD_ATTRS`. Attackers can exploit these unblocked serialization sinks to corrupt or rewrite arbitrary local files.

findings.title: `ast.Name` and `ast.Attribute` verification checks are siloed, allowing trivial sandbox escapes
findings.desc: `BAD_NAMES` and `BAD_ATTRS` block lists strictly apply to specific node types without cross-checking. Attackers can easily bypass `BAD_ATTRS` via direct imports (e.g., `from pandas import read_pickle; read_pickle()`) and evade `BAD_NAMES` blocks via attribute calls (e.g., `pandas.eval(..., engine='python')`), enabling full RCE.

findings.title: Validation of `open` and `allow_pickle` arguments fails open
findings.desc: The AST validation checks require arguments to strictly be `ast.Constant` values. Invoking `open(f, mode=var)` with a variable, or bypassing keywords with `**kwargs`, causes the static checker to silently skip evaluate them, completely neutralizing read-only and static deserialization enforcement.

findings.title: Mode 1 evaluation lacks CPU and memory bounds for native limits
findings.desc: Mode 1 relies solely on a coarse `timeout 5` but lacks the `ulimit -v` used in Mode 2. Deeply nested left-associative exponent chains like `(((9**999)**999)**999)` pass the `MAX_EXP` AST check but will rapidly exhaust system RAM when natively computed, enabling uncontrolled out-of-memory DoS.

findings.title: Heredoc delimiter injection
findings.desc: Using `<<'EXPREOF'` to pass untrusted LLM-generated inputs allows immediate shell breakout. If the untrusted expression/script contains `EXPREOF` on a new line, it abruptly terminates the heredoc and executes subsequent lines as arbitrary system shell commands.

findings.title: AST type-dispatch allows name/attribute ban bypasses
findings.desc: `BAD_NAMES` is only verified on `ast.Name` nodes, and `BAD_ATTRS` only on `ast.Attribute` nodes. Attackers can import dangerous attributes directly (`from pandas import read_pickle` evaluated as `ast.Name`) or access dangerous names safely via attributes (`pandas.eval`), completely bypassing their respective bans.

findings.title: `open()` write restriction bypassed by non-constant modes
findings.desc: The manual restriction on `open()` modes only evaluates integer constants. Passing dynamically executed parameters, positionals implicitly mapping to args, or string concats (`open(f, mode='w'+'')`) results in `mode` evaluating to `None`, entirely bypassing the write block validation.

findings.title: `allow_pickle` deserialization bypasses
findings.desc: The `getattr(...) is True` rule uses strict object-identity comparison. Attackers can deserialize malicious pickle payloads by utilizing non-boolean truthy values (`allow_pickle=1`), passing it via boolean expressions (`allow_pickle=(1==1)`), or defining it implicitly as a positional argument.

findings.title: `operator` module bypasses dunder restrictions
findings.desc: Blocklist explicit dunder enforcement logic falls short against the allowed `operator` module native functionalities. Malicious inputs can utilize `operator.attrgetter("__class__.__base__.__subclasses__")()` to dynamically traverse Python's object graph via explicit string arguments resulting in full sandbox escape.

findings.title: `BAD_ATTRS` unintentionally disables core JSON functionality
findings.desc: Adding `"loads"` to `BAD_ATTRS` (intended to restrict `pickle.loads` or `np.loads`) effectively breaks parsing operations in the safely approved `json` module, making `json.loads(string)` syntactically invalid.
